title: COVID-19 Pandemic Causes Canada's Worst Annual GDP Decline on Record
reason: Confirmed on all material points via independent sources. Statistics Canada / CBC News confirm real GDP shrank 5.4% in 2020, the steepest annual decline since quarterly national accounts began in 1961. StatCan's Daily (June 30, 2020 release) confirms monthly GDP fell 7.5% in March 2020 and 11.6% in April 2020, described as the largest monthly decline since the series started. The C.D. Howe Institute's Business Cycle Council publication and CBC News confirm the Council formally declared Canada in recession on May 1, 2020, dating the recession's start to Q1 2020. The 2008-09 comparison checks out: search results show the 2008-09 financial crisis contraction was 2.92% (2009), consistent with the "roughly twice the size of...2.9% pullback" claim in the description (5.4% vs 2.9% ≈ 1.9x, reasonably described as "roughly twice"). All figures, dates, and the causal narrative (pandemic lockdowns from March 2020) align precisely with the event description.

verifications.reason: Confirmed by Statistics Canada's own official Daily release (Q4 2020 GDP release, published 2021-03-02): "In 2020, real GDP shrank 5.4%, the steepest annual decline since quarterly data were first recorded in 1961." Also confirmed independently by CBC News (2021-03-02): "2020 was the worst year on record for Canada's economy. It shrank by 5.4%." The monthly collapse figures are confirmed exactly by StatCan's April 2020 industry GDP release: "Real gross domestic product (GDP) dropped 11.6% in April, following a 7.5% decline in March... the largest monthly decline since the series started in 1961." The C.D. Howe Institute Business Cycle Council recession declaration is confirmed by both CBC News and C.D. Howe's own publication page: the Council declared on May 1, 2020 that Canada had entered a recession (dated to Q1 2020, i.e., the recession call came in May 2020 as described). The only soft spot: multiple independent sources (StatCan historical retrospectives, Bank of Canada) put the 2008-09 annual GDP decline at approximately 2.5% (with 2.9% actually being the 1982 recession's figure, and peak-to-trough 2008-09 quarterly decline being ~3.3%), rather than exactly 2.9% as stated for the comparison. This is a minor precision issue in a secondary comparison figure, not in the core claim, and the qualitative comparison ("roughly twice the size") still holds under any of these reference figures (5.4% vs ~2.5-3.3%). Given the primary claims (5.4% annual decline, steepest since 1961, monthly declines of 7.5%/11.6%, C.D. Howe recession declaration in May 2020) are all verified directly against Statistics Canada's own official statistical releases plus independent news corroboration, I judge this materially accurate as described.
